questions.q: What does GitHub's REST API use to tell your client the URL of the next page?
options: A "next_url" field inside the JSON body
A real HTTP Link response header with rel="next"
You must always guess by incrementing the page number yourself
An email notification
questions.explain: GitHub returns a Link header with rel="next" (and rel="last", etc.) pointing to the exact next-page URL.

questions.q: In Stripe's cursor-based pagination, what does has_more: false mean?
options: The request failed
There are no items in the response at all
You've reached the end of the list — no more pages to fetch
You need to retry with a different limit
questions.explain: has_more is a boolean indicating whether another page exists; false means this page is the end of the list.

questions.q: In Stripe's pagination, what value do you pass as starting_after to get the next page?
options: The page number
A timestamp
The total count of items
The id of the last object from the previous page
questions.explain: starting_after is a cursor — the ID of the last object you saw — not a page number or timestamp.

questions.q: What real problem does cursor-based pagination avoid that page-number pagination can suffer from?
options: It avoids needing authentication
It avoids skipping or repeating items when the underlying list changes between requests
It avoids needing a limit parameter
It avoids returning JSON
questions.explain: Because a cursor is tied to a specific object, not a position, items added or removed mid-list don't shift later pages the way offset-based page numbers can.

questions.q: Why does pagination exist at all?
options: Because JSON cannot represent more than 100 items
To improve response compression
So a server never has to send (and a client never has to process) an unbounded result set in one response
It's required by the HTTP specification
questions.explain: Pagination splits large result sets into manageable pages fetched one request at a time, rather than one enormous response.
